name: Hana Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Hana, thanks for your time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say is confidential. Shall we begin?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, go ahead. I've got about an hour before my next phone booking.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Then tell me about a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do two kinds of work. In the mornings I do certified translations from Hindi and Gujarati into English for a small translation bureau: birth certificates, marriage certificates, bank statements, mostly for immigration and visa cases. A certified translation is one where a translator signs a statement that it's accurate, so a government office will accept it. In the afternoons I do telephone interpreting for the council and some doctors' surgeries, so a grandmother can explain her chest pain to a GP. I'm on the phone in my headset, walking around the flat.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the phone work because it's never the same twice. Last week I had a man trying to explain to the council that his landlord had taken the boiler out, and the word he used was a village word I'd only heard from my nani, my grandmother. What wears me out is the certificates: the stamps, the handwriting, checking every date three times. I'm still slow at those, and the senior translator at the bureau, Mrs Shah, has to review everything I sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right, honestly. That's what I'd guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and not much more. I'd say that to Dev, my partner, mostly, because he tests software and he's always going on about AI. I'm not big on posting things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. Government offices still want a human signature on a certified translation, and nobody wants a machine on the line with a scared patient. I already use an AI tool now and then for a quick first pass on non-certified letters, and it saves me twenty minutes, not my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, and keep using the AI tool for the boring letters. I'd ask Mrs Shah to let me sign more certificates without her review, which would raise my pay. And I'd keep paying extra off our mortgage, maybe 200 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Really calm. Our flat's small but we own most of it, and we've got about eight months put away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the signature mean in money, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Certificates I can sign alone pay about forty percent more than ones Mrs Shah has to check. Getting signed off to certify on my own is the only promotion a freelancer like me really gets. It'd take maybe a year if I'm careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anyone you'd worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Maybe Dev, a bit, because testing is the kind of thing these tools are good at. But in this picture even his job is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. That one makes me think of Dev more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is fine for paperwork, but official documents and health calls need a person who can be held responsible. I'd say it to friends, and I'd probably sign a petition about interpreters in hospitals if someone sent one. I wouldn't start one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the phone interpreting goes first. Councils love saving money, and an AI interpreter on the phone is cheap. Certificates last longer because of the signature, but the bureau might need fewer of us, and Mrs Shah could sign machine work herself. And Dev's testing job is right in the middle of that card, so it's both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard to become a sworn translator, which is a legal status where my signature is accepted by courts. That's an exam and about a year of evenings. I'd use the AI tools more for drafts, since everyone else will. And we'd save harder, maybe 500 a month between us, and hold off on the new car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, in the background all the time. Not panicked, but I'd be doing sums in my head on the bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Dev actually say to each other that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd sit with the laptop and do the spreadsheet, because that's how Dev copes. I'd say, 'If one of us goes, the other carries it.' My partner Dev would say his job will be fine, and I'd know he didn't believe it either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the AI tools more. Doesn't that speed up the thing you're worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. But if I don't, I'm just the slow one, and the slow one goes first. I'd rather be the person who uses it well and signs at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. For both of us. Oh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to look after people who did everything right and still lose out. I'd say that to family and friends. I'm not political, but I'd vote for whoever had an actual plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's both our jobs gone at about the same time. A signature is just a rule, and rules change when the machine is better than Mrs Shah. Dev and I are both thinking workers, so we don't even get the three extra years people with hands-on jobs get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents straight away about their sweet shop, because that's hands-on work, and the robots come about three years after the AI. I'd stop all spending that isn't food and the mortgage. And I'd think seriously about selling our flat and moving back to my parents' town, where things are cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My chest goes tight thinking about it. Two of us, one flat, no time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would working in the sweet shop mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting up at five to make jalebi with my dad, serving at the counter, doing the orders for weddings. My dad has wanted me in the family sweet shop since I was twelve. I'd be going back to what I spent a whole degree avoiding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you tell first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, and she'd be kind about it. Then my dad would say 'I told you,' and then he'd find me an apron.

I'd **vote** for whoever had an actual plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still both of us, but some time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should prepare now, as a country. I'd say it at family dinners, which are loud enough already. I'd want the schools to start teaching kids about this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years means we'd both lose our jobs around 2031, but with time to arrange it. I'd still do the sworn translator exam, because three or four years of better pay is worth it. And it changes when we have children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Dev about having a baby sooner, maybe next year, while we both have work and parental leave. We'd pay down as much of the mortgage as we can, maybe 600 a month. And I'd start helping at my parents' shop on Saturdays, so I learn it before I need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but organised. It's a list, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would AI change when you have children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd want a baby while there's still a salary and leave to take. If we wait until we're thirty and the jobs are gone, it gets harder. It sounds cold, but I'd rather be honest with myself about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Saturdays at the shop on top of everything. What gives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My Saturday lie-ins, and seeing friends. I'd miss them, but my mum would feed me, so it's not all bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a lot more normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time enough if people take it seriously, and I'd say that to anyone who's panicking. I'd be the calm one at family dinners for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have a proper career first. Sworn translator by 2028, good pay, kids, and then a change in my mid-thirties. Dev would have time to move into something too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, get the sworn status, and use the AI tools as they get better. We'd save steadily, 300 a month. I'd keep an eye on it each year and decide around 2032 whether to move into the shop or something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a low way. It's there, but it doesn't run my day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own kids about work, in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kids to learn to do something with their hands as well as their heads. My nani could sew a whole wedding outfit in a week. That'll be worth something when the computers do everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Dev worry less too, in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less, yes. He'd probably move into whatever the new tech jobs are, because he's quicker than me with that. I'd follow a bit behind, which suits me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Dev and I would lose our jobs at the same time and we'd have no time to arrange anything. What would help is support for households where both people are hit at once, and keeping the rule that a human signs official translations for as long as possible.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the grandmothers on the phone. When an old woman explains her chest pain to a GP, she's also checking whether someone on the line cares. I don't know if a machine can do that part.
